```{r}
#| echo: false


library(knitr)
library(formatR)
library(tidyverse)
library(gganimate)
library(gifski)
opts_chunk$set(out.width = '100%', options(width=60))

opts_knit$set(global.par = TRUE)
opts_chunk$set(echo=FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, comment = '', class.output='sh',
               fig.width=8, fig.height=5, fig.align = "center")

my_red <- "#E41A1C"
my_blue <- "#377EB8"
my_green <- "#4DAF4A"
my_purple <- "#984EA3"
my_orange <- "#FF7F00"
my_yellow <- "#FFFF33"
my_red2 <- "#FBB4AE" 
my_blue2 <- "#B3CDE3" 
my_green2 <- "#CCEBC5" 
my_purple2 <- "#DECBE4"
my_orange2 <- "#FED9A6"
my_yellow2 <- "#FFFFCC"


dat <- read.csv("../../data/McCrea.csv") |> 
  mutate(Cond = recode(as_factor(Cond), 
                       "1" = "self-handicap", 
                       "2" = "control"))

means <- dat |> group_by(Cond) |>
  summarize(mean = mean(percent))

sds <- dat |> group_by(Cond) |>
  summarize(sd = sd(percent))

ns <- dat |> group_by(Cond) |>
  summarize(n = n())

## extract x_bar1, x_bar2, s1, s2, n1, and n2
x_bar1 <- means$mean[1]
x_bar2 <- means$mean[2]
s1 <- sds$sd[1]
s2 <- sds$sd[2]
n1 <- ns$n[1]
n2 <- ns$n[2]

s2p <- ((n1 - 1) * s1^2 + (n2 - 1) * s2^2)/(n1 + n2 - 2)
sp <- sqrt(s2p)
t_crit <- qt(.025, df = n1 + n2 - 2, lower.tail = FALSE)
```

## Last APA Writeup

A two-tailed Welch-Satterthwaite $t$-test with $\alpha = .05$ indicated a significant difference between conditions, $t(51.9) = -2.29, p = .026$. Participants in the self-handicap condition correctly answered a lower percentage of items ($N = 32, M = .47, SD = .17$) than participants in the control condition ($N = 29, M = .58, SD = .22$), 95% CI of the difference $= [0.01, 0.22]$.

[The observed difference between groups was $.58 - .47 = .11$. This is an **effect size**]{.fragment}

-   [**Effect size:** a statistical **estimate** of a **magnitude** of an effect rather than a **test**]{.fragment}

[**Problem:** How should we interpret this effect size?]{.fragment}

## Standardized Effect Size

In a vacuum, **raw** effect sizes are difficult to interpret and compare to one another

-   Often because the scale of the original variable(s) can be hard to directly interpret
-   What difference in proportion would be considered large?
-   **Standardized** effect sizes put all effect sizes on a common scale to aid interpretation and comparison

## Two Families

::::: {.columns .v-center-container}
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../../Figs/corleone.png)
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
![](../../Figs/sopranos.png)
:::
:::::

[Not that type of family!]{.fragment}

## Two Families of Effect

The $D$-family

-   Refers to standardized **differences** (or ratios)
-   Cohen's $d$
-   Risk, Odds, and Risk and Odds Ratios

The $R$-family

-   Refers to standardized **associations**
-   Correlation (standardized covariance)
-   $R^2$, $\eta^2$, $\omega^2$
-   $W$ and Cramer's $V$

## Cohen's $d$

::: {style="font-size: 0.9em;"}
General form:

$$d = \frac{\text{raw difference}}{\text{standard deviation}}$$

**Interpretation:** Transforms **raw difference** into $Z$ (standard deviation) units
:::

::::::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}
:::::: {.columns .v-center-container}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**One Sample**

$$d = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s_x}$$

Difference between observed and null hypothesized mean divided by standard deviation
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**Paired Sample**

$$d = \frac{\bar{D}}{s_D}$$

Difference in paired sample means divided by standard deviation
:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**Independent Samples**

$$d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p}$$

Difference in sample means divided by pooled standard deviation

-   Can use other SDs besides pooled depending on desired interpretation
:::
::::::
:::::::

## Subtle Clarification

$t$-test statistics and Cohen's $d$ have similar forms. They often have the same numerator, but slightly different denominators

- $t$-statistics divide by the standard **error**




::::::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}
:::::: {.columns .v-center-container}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**One Sample**

$$t_{\bar{x}} = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s_\bar{x}}$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**Paired Sample**

$$t_{\bar{D}} = \frac{\bar{D}}{s_\bar{D}}$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**Independent Samples**

$$t_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}}$$

:::
::::::
:::::::

- $d$-effect sizes divide by standard **deviation**


::::::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}
:::::: {.columns .v-center-container}
::: {.column width="33%"}
**One Sample**

$$d = \frac{\bar{x} - \mu_0}{s_x}$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**Paired Sample**

$$d = \frac{\bar{D}}{s_D}$$

:::

::: {.column width="33%"}
**Independent Samples**

$$d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p}$$
:::
::::::
:::::::


## Example

**Original Study**:

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}
McCrea, S. M. (2008). Self-handicapping, excuse making, and counterfactual thinking: Consequences for self-esteem and future motivation. *Journal of Personality and Social Psychology*, *2*, 274-292.
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.95em;"}
**Replication study link**: <https://osf.io/2kjgz>

**Step 1**: Subject took a math exam and were told that they scored in the 35th percentile of university students

**Step 2**: Subjects saw statements supposedly written by previous participants

-   Self-handicap group: half of statements indicated that more practice would have improved their performance, half of statements were neutral

-   Control group: all statements were neutral

**Step 3**: Subjects took a second surprise math exam
:::


## Example

As a reminder, our means $\bar{x}_1$ and $\bar{x}_2$ were (`R` objects were saved from previous slides):

```{r}
#| echo: true

x_bar1
x_bar2
```

And our pooled standard deviation $s_p$

```{r}
#| echo: true

sp
```



## $d$-Effect size

$$d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p}$$

```{r}
#| echo: true

(d <- (x_bar1 - x_bar2)/sp)

```


**Interpretation:** The mean number of correctly answered questions was 0.59 SDs lower in the self-handicap condition than in the control condition.

- All we did was convert our difference into SDs instead of the total number of correctly answered questions

## Confidence Interval for $d$

Cohen's $d$ changes our original units to $Z$-score units.

What is the standard deviation for $Z$-scores?

- [1]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}

So if we plug in $s_p =$ [1]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"} what would our confidence interval look like?

::::: {.content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}
::::{ .fragment}
:::{.answer}

$s_{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2} = s_p \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}$

So if we plug in $s_p = 1$

$\text{statistic} \pm \text{critical value} \times \text{standard error} = d \pm t_{crit} \times \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_1} + \frac{1}{n_2}}$

```{r}
#| echo: true
d - t_crit * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2)
d + t_crit * sqrt(1/n1 + 1/n2)

```

:::
::::
:::::

## Benchmarks

Jacob Cohen (another very important/famous statistician) proposed the following (very loose!) benchmarks for $d$:

-   $d \approx .2$ is a small effect
-   $d \approx .5$ is a medium effect
-   $d \approx .8$ is a large effect

These are rough point estimates

- $d = .1$ would be *very small*
- $d = .3$ is small-to-medium

Just use this as a way to orient yourself, not as an objective rule


## Full APA Writeup

A two-tailed Welch-Satterthwaite $t$-test with $\alpha = .05$ indicated a significant difference between conditions, $t(51.9) = -2.29, p = .026$. Participants in the self-handicap condition correctly answered a lower percentage of items ($N = 32, M = .47, SD = .17$) than participants in the control condition ($N = 29, M = .58, SD = .22$), 95% CI of the difference $= [0.01, 0.22]$, Cohen's $d = 0.60$, 95% CI($d$) = $[0.08, 1.11]$.

## In `R`

The `effectsize` package has lots of handy functions for calculating effect sizes, including a `cohens_d()` function that uses syntax just like the `t.test()` function.

```{r}
#| echo: true
library(effectsize)
cohens_d(percent ~ Cond, data = dat)

```

## Practice

Two classes of students, each $N = 21$, were assigned a different math curriculum, curriculum A or curriculum B. They each then took the same final exam. Students in the curriculum A class got an average score of 80 with a standard deviation of 8. Students in the curriculum B class got an average score of 77 with a standard deviation of 5. What is Cohen's $d$?



[$s_p = \sqrt{\frac{(n_1 -1)s^2_1 + n_2 -1)s^2_2}{n_1 + n_2 -2}} = \sqrt{\frac{(21 -1)8^2 + 21-1)5^2}{21 + 21 -2}} = 6.67$]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}


[$d = \frac{\bar{x}_1 - \bar{x}_2}{s_p} = \frac{80-77}{6.67} = 0.45$]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}

## Risk and Odds

::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}
Risk and Odds are ratio-based $d$-family effect sizes for categorical variables

Below are some results from the Moderna Phase 3 clinical trial of the mRNA-1273 COVID vaccine (November, 2020)
:::

::: {style="font-size: 0.6em;"}
Baden, L. R., El Sahly, H. M., Essink, B., Kotloff, K., Frey, S., Novak, R., ... & Zaks, T. (2021). Efficacy and safety of the mRNA-1273 SARS-CoV-2 vaccine. *New England Journal of Medicine*, *384*(5), 403-416.
:::

:::::: {style="font-size: 0.7em;"}
|             | **COVID-19** | **No COVID-19** | **Total**  |
|:------------|:------------:|:---------------:|:----------:|
| **Vaccine** |      11      |     14,123      |   14,134   |
| **Placebo** |     185      |     13,888      |   14,073   |
| **Total**   |   **196**    |   **28,011**    | **28,207** |

::::: {.columns .v-center-container}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Risk** is the conditional probability of one outcome for a group

-   Risk(COVID-19 \| Vaccine) $= \frac{11}{14,134} = .0008 = .08\%$

-   Risk(COVID-19 \| Placebo) $= \frac{185}{14,073} = .0131 = 1.31\%$
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Odds** is the ratio of one outcome to another outcome for a group

-   Odds(COVID-19 \| Vaccine) $= \frac{11}{14,123} = .0008$

-   Odds(COVID-19 \| Placebo) $= \frac{185}{13,888} = .0133$
:::
:::::
::::::

## More Risk and Odds

:::::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}
|             | **COVID-19** | **No COVID-19** | **Total**  |
|:------------|:------------:|:---------------:|:----------:|
| **Vaccine** |      11      |     14,123      |   14,134   |
| **Placebo** |     185      |     13,888      |   14,073   |
| **Total**   |   **196**    |   **28,011**    | **28,207** |

::::: {.columns .v-center-container}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Risk** uses total \# in vaccine group as the denominator

-   Risk(COVID-19 \| Vaccine) $= \frac{11}{14,134} = .0008 = .08\%$

-   Conditional probability
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Odds** uses \# of vaccinated individuals who did not contract COVID-19 as the denominator

-   Odds(COVID-19 \| Vaccine) $= \frac{11}{14,123} = .0008$

-   If outcomes are equally probable, odds = 1
:::
:::::
::::::

Risk and odds are not always similar - here they are because getting COVID-19 (in the given time frame) is highly unlikely in either group.

## Risk Ratio

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

|             | **COVID-19** | **No COVID-19** | **Total**  |
|:------------|:------------:|:---------------:|:----------:|
| **Vaccine** |      11      |     14,123      |   14,134   |
| **Placebo** |     185      |     13,888      |   14,073   |
| **Total**   |   **196**    |   **28,011**    | **28,207** |



**Risk ratio** (also known as **relative risk**)

$$\text{Risk ratio} = \frac{\text{Risk (COVID-19 | Placebo)}}{\text{Risk (COVID-19 | Vaccine)}}$$ $$= \left(\frac{185}{14,073}\right) \bigg/ \left(\frac{11}{14,134}\right) = 16.89$$

- The risk of contracting COVID-19 without a vaccine is 16.89$\times$ higher than if you get the Moderna vaccine

- If the two risks are equal, then the risk ratio equals 1

:::

## Odds Ratio

**Odds ratio**

$$\text{Odds ratio}  = \frac{\text{Odds (COVID-19 | Placebo)}}{\text{Odds (COVID-19 | Vaccine)}}$$ $$= \left(\frac{185}{13,388}\right) \bigg/ \left(\frac{11}{14,123}\right) = 17.10$$

The odds of contracting COVID-19 without a vaccine is over 17$\times$ higher than if you get the Moderna vaccine

## Risk vs. Odds

In our example, risk (ratio) and odds (ratio) gave us very similar answers.

Mathematically, the difference between risk and odds is what quantity goes in the denominator

**Risk** of COVID-19 among vaccinated participants:

-   .08% of those vaccinated contracted COVID-19

-   1.31% of those unvaccinated contracted COVID-19

-   Risks are probabilities: range from 0 to 1

## Odds vs. Risk

**Odds** of contracting COVID-19 in vaccine condition:

-   Among those vaccinated, the ratio of those who contracted COVID-19 to those who did not attack is .008

-   Odds $\approx$ 1 indicate roughly equally likely outcomes

-   Odds \> 1 indicates higher probability for the group in the numerator

-   Odds \< 1 indicates higher probability for the group in the denominator

-   The odds of **no** COVID-19 for those vaccinated is $\frac{14,123}{11} = 1284$

-   The odds of **no** COVID-19 for those unvaccinated is $\frac{13,888}{185} = 75$

    -   A vaccinated person is 1284$\times$ more likely to *not* contract COVID-19 than to do so, whereas an unvaccinated person is only 75$\times$ more likely to *not* (in study's given time frame, pre-variants)


## Practice

::: {style="font-size: 0.8em;"}

This contingency table compares the success rate of getting accepted by a PhD program depending on whether students did undergraduate research.


|             | **Accepted** | **Rejected** | **Total**  |
|:------------|:------------:|:---------------:|:----------:|
| **Research** |      85      |     50     |   135   |
| **No Research** |    22      |     91      |   113   |
| **Total**   |   **107**    |   **141**    | **248** |


What is the **risk ratio** of getting rejected for a student who did no research versus one who did? 

[$\text{Risk ratio} = \frac{\text{Risk (rejected | no research)}}{\text{Risk (rejected | research)}} = \left(\frac{91}{113}\right) \bigg/ \left(\frac{50}{135}\right) = 2.17$]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}

What is the **odds ratio** of getting rejected for a student who did no research versus one who did?


[$\text{Odds ratio}  = \frac{\text{Odds (rejected | no research)}}{\text{Odds (rejected | research)}}= \left(\frac{91}{22}\right) \bigg/ \left(\frac{50}{85}\right) = 7.03$]{.answer .fragment .content-visible unless-meta="params.v0"}

:::
